title: Raga Todi
hookLine: a morning raga that opens by admitting need

cards: The first minutes after waking are strange ones. The armor isn't on yet.
Before the to-do list and the phone and the public face, there's a softer person blinking at the ceiling, who might, for a moment, say what they actually need.

Tradition calls today's raga a morning raga, and a tender one. And the hymn that opens it sounds like that unguarded minute: no ceremony, no long praise, just an honest sentence about need. Today: Raga Todi.

teach.b: Todi comes after Jaitsri in the Granth's order. Its first hymn is by Guru Ram Das, mahala four. It begins: har bin reh na sakai man mera.

teach.h: WITHOUT THE LORD, MY MIND CANNOT LIVE.
teach.b: In paraphrase: without the Lord, my mind cannot live. No argument, no description of God's greatness, just dependence, the way a child says I need you.

teach.h: THE BELOVED, THE BREATH OF MY LIFE.
teach.b: That line opens the refrain, the rahao, the part the hymn keeps coming back to, and it goes on, in paraphrase: my beloved, the breath of my life, is the Lord; the Guru has brought me to meet him, and I won't be tossed again on the terrifying ocean of the world.
Notice the order. First the need, said plainly. Then the beloved, named as breath, as close as the air going in and out.
Then the meeting, and the steadiness that follows. That's what tender means here. Not weak, not sentimental.
Tender is how a person sounds when they stop pretending to be self-sufficient. Tradition sets Todi in the morning, and teachers describe raga moods in different ways, so hold the hour lightly.
But you can hear why these words would sit well at dawn, before the armor goes on.

how: Shabads from the Todi section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Raga Todi in kirtan, including in morning programs at some gurdwaras, following the tradition that links Todi with the morning.

games.why: har bin reh na sakai man mera: the opening line is a confession of need, said as plainly as a child would.

practice: Let the shoulders drop, unclench the jaw, and rest the hands open, palms up, breathing as if you'd just woken. Then quietly finish this sentence for yourself, without explaining it: without this, I couldn't live.
A person, a faith, the breath itself; if you pray, the answer can be Waheguru.
